demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Anant is eighty years old, a widower who served forty years with the Coast Guard, and for most of his life, his pride was anchored to the uniform he wore. That changed six months ago on a squally Tuesday in October. He was volunteering, skippering a small tour boat for a local conservation society off the coast of Maine. The fog had rolled in thick and fast, a sudden grey wall that swallowed the horizon. He was navigating by instruments, confident in his decades of experience, when the impact came—a sickening crunch of fibreglass and a high, sharp scream. He had struck a small pleasure craft, nearly invisible in the haze. The young woman at its helm was thrown against the console, her leg shattered. The memory of her pale, shocked face as the paramedics worked, the wail of the sirens echoing across the water, is the last clear thing he remembers from that day.

In the weeks that followed, the event refused to settle into a coherent story in his mind. When Anant tried to deliberately recall the sequence of events, he found only a frustrating void. Yet, the memory would ambush him in other ways, not as a narrative but as a sensory assault. The smell of salt and diesel, the specific shade of grey of the fog, the jarring thud that seemed to reverberate up through the soles of his feet—these fragments would erupt without warning, feeling utterly and terrifyingly real. After one of these sensory flashbacks, he is left hyper-alert, and the world seems full of echoes of the trauma; the sound of wind in the pines or the damp smell of his basement becomes a potential harbinger of the memory's return. This terrifying reliving of disconnected moments only heightened his sense of constant, unpredictable danger. He began to feel that he had to be on guard at all times, because an attack could come from anywhere, even from within his own mind. His home, once a sanctuary, became a place of potential ambushes. He started choosing his chair in the living room based on its view of the door and window, a habit he couldn't explain but couldn't break.

The triggers are everywhere. A walk in the state park behind his house, once his greatest pleasure, is now a minefield; the damp, earthy smell and the sound of wind in the pines are too similar to the coastal headlands of that day. This immersion in nature instantly brings back shards of the memory—the splintered wood, the cry—and with them, a surge of adrenaline that tells him he is unsafe. He finds himself scanning the trees, his heart pounding, before retreating back to his car. Even the sound of a distant ambulance siren sends a jolt of terror through him, activating a profound sense of threat that makes him feel as though disaster is imminent. That piercing wail on the wind is not just a warning of external danger; it has become a personal judgment, confirming his belief that he is now fundamentally unsafe to be around. In these moments of heightened alert, the memories become more accessible, more vivid, as if his brain is trying to find the source of the danger in the past. This constant sense of being on guard has, over time, cemented a devastating conclusion in his mind: the world is a dangerous place, and he is no longer competent to navigate it.

This belief has become the lens through which he sees everything. His conviction that he is no longer competent means that things he once would have registered and dismissed—the low rumble of a boat engine, a patch of morning fog—now snag his attention, standing out as potential signs of another failure. He has come to believe the accident wasn't just a mistake born of fog and bad luck, but a reflection of a fundamental flaw in his character. "A good man, a careful man, wouldn't have let that happen," he repeats to himself. This painful appraisal—that there is something wrong with him as a person—is a constant, heavy presence. Whenever the memory of the woman's pale, shocked face comes to mind, he immediately tries to forcefully push the image away or tells himself the event wasn't real, desperate to stop the sensory replay before it can take hold. It makes any conversation about the future, especially his grandchildren's, feel like a personal indictment, a reminder of the future he nearly stole from that young woman. To escape the acute shame of these thoughts, Anant has developed a series of frantic mental maneuvers. He tries to forcefully push the images out of his head, or he tells himself the event didn't really happen, that it was just a terrible dream. Sometimes he forces himself to think only of positive things, like his late wife’s smile, in a desperate attempt to paper over the horror.

But these strategies are failing. Trying to suppress the memories only seems to make them stronger, and the effort leaves him exhausted and more attuned to his triggers. The constant feeling of threat forces him to avoid any unfamiliar places, shrinking his world to his house and the corner store. This avoidance has become a trap; by never testing his fear, he has no way to learn that the world is not as dangerous as his body insists it is, and so the feeling of threat remains perpetually high. The magical thinking, his attempt to deny reality, only deepens his conviction that he is defective, because a sane person, he reasons, wouldn't have to lie to himself to get through the day. The entire system now feeds itself. A trigger, like a siren, creates a sense of threat, which dredges up a memory fragment. The memory reinforces his negative belief that he is a dangerous person, which is so painful he must use a strategy like thought suppression to cope. But the suppression leaves the memory unprocessed and sharp, ready to be activated by the next trigger, which his hypervigilant state is now actively scanning for. His life has become a tightening loop of fear and self-blame. He finally sought help last week after his eldest grandson, a high school senior, announced he was thinking of enlisting in the Coast Guard. Anant couldn't conjure a single positive word. He just stared, his mind filled with the sound of splintering fibreglass, and had to leave the room. He is terrified that this thing inside him will not only consume his past, but also destroy his connection to his family's future.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not state that triggers directly cause negative beliefs about himself or the world.
The vignette does not state that his negative beliefs cause him to be more aware of or search for triggers.
The vignette does not state that the trauma memory directly causes him to use maladaptive coping strategies.
The vignette does not state that experiencing the trauma memory makes him more sensitive or attentive to triggers.
The vignette does not state that using maladaptive strategies increases his overall sense of threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not state that triggers directly cause negative beliefs about himself or the world.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not state that his negative beliefs cause him to be more aware of or search for triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not state that the trauma memory directly causes him to use maladaptive coping strategies.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not state that experiencing the trauma memory makes him more sensitive or attentive to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not state that using maladaptive strategies increases his overall sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
